title: AES Encryption
subtitle: Advanced Encryption Standard: blocks, keys, and rounds

whyItExists.problem: Before AES, the aging DES cipher (56-bit keys) was broken by brute force in 1998. NIST needed a modern, strong symmetric cipher that could be used worldwide.
whyItExists.solution: NIST ran a public competition (1997-2001). Rijndael, submitted by Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen, won and became AES. It is now the global standard for symmetric encryption.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Encrypting files, database fields, API payloads, full-disk encryption. AES-256-GCM for new code.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Password storage (use Argon2 instead). Signing/authentication only (use HMAC). Very small IoT devices with no hardware AES (consider ChaCha20).

explainModes.beginner: AES is like a combination lock with a 256-bit combination. It scrambles your data using that combination, and you need the exact same combination to unscramble it.
explainModes.simple: AES takes a 128-bit block of data and applies 14 rounds of substitutions, shifts, and mixing operations. The key determines what the rounds do — same key means same output every time.
explainModes.standard: AES is a symmetric block cipher: same key encrypts and decrypts, operates on 128-bit (16-byte) blocks, supports 128/192/256-bit keys. AES-256 is recommended for new systems. Must be used with a mode of operation (never raw 'AES ECB').
explainModes.technical: AES uses a substitution-permutation network: SubBytes (S-box substitution), ShiftRows (byte permutation), MixColumns (GF(2^8) matrix multiply), AddRoundKey. 10/12/14 rounds for 128/192/256-bit keys. The best known attack (biclique) reduces effective key size by 2 bits — no practical break.
explainModes.deepDive: AES has hardware acceleration on all modern CPUs (AES-NI on x86, ARMv8 AES extensions). This makes software AES comparable to hardware speed. The key schedule derives round keys from the main key; a weak key schedule was a DES flaw AES avoids. For large data, AES-GCM runs AES in counter mode and uses GHASH for authentication, both parallelisable.

content.text: AES is the global standard for symmetric (shared-key) encryption. It's used in TLS, full-disk encryption, Wi-Fi (WPA2/3), and countless storage systems. The same key encrypts and decrypts, making key distribution the main challenge.

items: Block size: always 128 bits (16 bytes) — fixed regardless of key size
No known practical attacks after 20+ years of cryptanalysis

content.definition: An encryption algorithm that operates on fixed-size blocks. AES processes exactly 16 bytes at a time. Longer messages require a mode of operation to chain blocks.

content.code:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers import Cipher, algorithms, modes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import padding
import os

key = os.urandom(32)   # AES-256: 32-byte key
iv  = os.urandom(16)   # 128-bit IV, one per message

# --- Encrypt ---
def aes_cbc_encrypt(key: bytes, iv: bytes, plaintext: bytes) -> bytes:
    # PKCS7 padding to align to 16 bytes
    padder = padding.PKCS7(128).padder()
    padded = padder.update(plaintext) + padder.finalize()

    cipher = Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.CBC(iv))
    encryptor = cipher.encryptor()
    return encryptor.update(padded) + encryptor.finalize()

# --- Decrypt ---
def aes_cbc_decrypt(key: bytes, iv: bytes, ciphertext: bytes) -> bytes:
    cipher = Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.CBC(iv))
    decryptor = cipher.decryptor()
    padded = decryptor.update(ciphertext) + decryptor.finalize()

    unpadder = padding.PKCS7(128).unpadder()
    return unpadder.update(padded) + unpadder.finalize()

# Usage
msg = b"Top secret message"
ciphertext = aes_cbc_encrypt(key, iv, msg)
print("Encrypted:", ciphertext.hex())
print("Decrypted:", aes_cbc_decrypt(key, iv, ciphertext))

content.text: AES-CBC does not authenticate the ciphertext. An attacker can modify the ciphertext undetected and potentially decrypt it via a padding oracle attack. For new code, use AES-GCM instead.

content.code:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
import os

key = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)  # 32-byte random key
nonce = os.urandom(12)                      # 12-byte nonce (96-bit, recommended for GCM)
aad = b"version:1,user:42"                 # optional associated data (authenticated but not encrypted)

aesgcm = AESGCM(key)

# Encrypt — produces ciphertext + 16-byte auth tag appended
ciphertext = aesgcm.encrypt(nonce, b"Sensitive data", aad)

# Decrypt — raises InvalidTag if anything was tampered with
try:
    plaintext = aesgcm.decrypt(nonce, ciphertext, aad)
    print("Decrypted:", plaintext)
except Exception:
    print("Tampering detected — authentication failed!")

a.name: AES-CBC
a.useWhen: Legacy systems; never for new code

b.name: AES-GCM
weaknesses: Nonce reuse is catastrophic (use random 96-bit nonce)
96-bit nonce limit per key (~2^32 messages safely)
b.useWhen: All new applications — the default choice

content.text: AES-256 provides ~128-bit post-quantum security (Grover's algorithm halves effective key size). This makes AES-256 a future-proof choice even when quantum computers exist.

questions.question: What block size does AES always use?
options: It varies with the key size
questions.explanation: AES always uses a 128-bit (16-byte) block size regardless of key length (128, 192, or 256 bits).

questions.question: Why is AES-GCM preferred over AES-CBC for new applications?
options: GCM provides both encryption and authentication; CBC provides encryption only
questions.explanation: GCM is an AEAD mode: it encrypts data AND appends an authentication tag. Any ciphertext modification causes decryption to fail with an InvalidTag error.

questions.question: What happens if you reuse a nonce with the same AES-GCM key?
options: An attacker can recover the plaintext and forge messages
Nothing — nonce reuse is harmless in GCM
questions.explanation: GCM nonce reuse is catastrophic: two messages encrypted with the same key+nonce XOR together, exposing both plaintexts and allowing the attacker to forge authentication tags.

faq.q: Should I use AES-128 or AES-256?
faq.a: AES-256 is recommended for new code. AES-128 has no known practical break, but AES-256 provides extra margin and post-quantum safety (128-bit quantum security vs 64-bit for AES-128).

faq.q: Should I use AES-CBC in new code?
faq.a: No. Use AES-GCM. AES-CBC does not authenticate the ciphertext, making it vulnerable to padding oracle attacks when used with PKCS7 padding and error messages.

faq.q: Does AES have any known weaknesses?
faq.a: No practical attacks exist. The best known attack (biclique) reduces effective key size by just 2 bits. After 20+ years of cryptanalysis, AES remains the gold standard.

examples: TLS 1.3 uses AES-256-GCM as its primary cipher suite
macOS FileVault encrypts the entire startup disk with AES-XTS-256
Signal Protocol uses AES-256-CBC for the message ratchet (now transitioning to GCM)
